title: Can't Get Out of Bed
summary: Navigate the heaviness of a morning when getting up feels impossible. Multiple paths through inertia—from total shutdown to tiny workable steps.

objectives.title: Get Out of Bed
objectives.description: Stand up and leave the bed

objectives.title: Complete One Task
objectives.description: Do at least one thing beyond getting up

objectives.title: Find a Tiny Step
objectives.description: Lower the bar to something achievable

objectives.title: Feet on Floor
objectives.description: Get your feet on the ground

objectives.title: Caught the Loop
objectives.description: Notice a thought pattern while it's happening

objectives.title: Lowered the Bar
objectives.description: Deliberately reduce expectations to something achievable

objectives.title: Second Attempt
objectives.description: Get up after collapsing back into bed

objectives.title: No Self-Attack
objectives.description: Get up without engaging the self-critical voice

routes.name: Gradual Activation
routes.description: Built momentum through sequential small steps—sit, feet down, stand, one task
routes.transferMapping: Tomorrow morning: sit up, feet down, stand, one small task. Sequence matters.

routes.name: Radical Lowering
routes.description: Found the smallest possible step and started there—one leg, ten seconds, just water
routes.transferMapping: Find the smallest possible task: just put feet on floor, just drink water, just stand for 10 seconds

routes.name: The Kinder Path
routes.description: Used self-compassion to counter the inner critic and enable action
routes.transferMapping: When you hear 'what's wrong with you': say 'I'm struggling. That's what this is.'

routes.name: Supported Movement
routes.description: Reached out for help and used connection to enable activation
routes.transferMapping: Set up a morning accountability text with someone who will check in

routes.name: The Second Try
routes.description: Collapsed back into bed, then found a way to try again with a gentler approach
routes.discoveryHint: What happens if you don't stay down after falling?
routes.transferMapping: If you collapse back into bed, give yourself 5 minutes, then try a smaller step

routes.name: Pattern Spotter
routes.description: Noticed the thought loops while they were happening
routes.transferMapping: Name the pattern out loud when you notice it: 'There's the self-attack script again'

routes.name: Partial Is Progress
routes.description: Accepted that less than everything still counts
routes.transferMapping: Define 'enough' before you start: what's the minimum that counts today?

routes.name: The Heavy Day
routes.description: Stayed in bed—the weight was too much today
routes.transferMapping: Tomorrow: set up one tiny step before you go to sleep tonight

routes.name: Too Much Too Fast
routes.description: Tried to do the full routine and crashed from overreach
routes.discoveryHint: What happens when you demand everything?
routes.transferMapping: Before starting, ask: Is this the smallest version? Can I do even less?

routes.name: The Inner Critic Wins
routes.description: Let the self-attack pattern drive behavior into shutdown
routes.transferMapping: Notice the self-attack voice and name it: 'That's the critic, not the truth'

routes.name: The Perfectionism Trap
routes.description: All-or-nothing thinking collapsed partial progress into nothing
routes.transferMapping: When 'not enough' appears, ask: Is this observation or all-or-nothing thinking?

challenges.title: No Collapse
challenges.description: Get up and stay up—don't fall back into bed at any point
challenges.transferFocus: Tomorrow, commit to staying up once you're up—even if it's just for 10 minutes

challenges.title: Minimum Viable Morning
challenges.description: Complete at least one task without overreaching
challenges.transferFocus: Define minimum viable before you start: what's the absolute least that counts?

challenges.title: Silence the Critic
challenges.description: Get up without engaging self-attack patterns
challenges.transferFocus: Notice the first self-attack thought and name it: 'There's the critic'

challenges.title: Baby Steps
challenges.description: Get up using only the smallest possible increments
challenges.transferFocus: Find the smallest possible step—just wiggle one toe, just open one eye

challenges.title: Fall and Rise
challenges.description: Collapse back into bed, then recover and get up anyway
challenges.transferFocus: If you collapse back, set a 5-minute timer. Then try a smaller step.

challenges.title: Kinder Words
challenges.description: Use self-compassion as the primary activation strategy
challenges.transferFocus: Speak to yourself like you'd speak to a struggling friend

challenges.title: No Scrolling
challenges.description: Get up without retreating to phone scrolling
challenges.transferFocus: Put your phone across the room before bed—make scrolling require getting up

challenges.title: Reach Out Early
challenges.description: Text someone before attempting to get up, then get up with their support
challenges.transferFocus: Set up a morning accountability text with someone before you go to sleep

nodes.text:
You're awake. You know because the ceiling is there and your eyes are open.

The alarm went off ten minutes ago. Or twenty. Time moves strangely when you're lying here.

Your body feels like it's made of concrete. Not tired exactly—you slept. This is something else. A heaviness that has nothing to do with sleep. The day is out there waiting, and you already know you don't have what it takes to meet it.

The thought of standing up is overwhelming. Not the standing itself. The everything that comes after.

You push yourself toward sitting. Your arms feel weak—not physically, but in some other way. Like the signal from your brain isn't getting through clearly.

You make it halfway. Propped on your elbows, staring at the wall.

This is harder than it should be. The voice in your head has opinions about that.

Okay. What's the smallest thing you could do?

Not get up. Not shower. Not face the day. Just... something smaller than that.

Your brain offers options: open your eyes wider. Move one leg. Sit up for ten seconds. Text someone that you're struggling.

All of them feel like climbing a mountain. But some mountains are smaller than others.

You reach for your phone. The light hurts your eyes but you don't put it down.

Scrolling. Nothing registers. You're not reading, you're just... moving your thumb. Time passes. Fifteen minutes. Thirty. The world outside gets brighter.

Your body hasn't moved. Part of you knows this isn't helping. Another part doesn't care.

You pull the covers over your head. The world gets smaller. Darker. Safer.

This is what you do. Hide from the day until the day goes away. Except it doesn't go away. It just waits.

Under here, you can pretend nothing exists. You can pretend you don't have to be a person today. The relief is real. The cost comes later.

You're sitting up. Feet not on the floor yet, but vertical. That's something.

The room looks the same as always. Clothes on the chair you meant to put away. Light coming through the curtains. A day that exists whether you participate in it or not.

Your brain is already suggesting you lie back down. It would be so easy. Just fall backward. The bed is right there.

You moved one leg. Just slightly. Toward the edge of the bed.

It's absurd how much that took. A person who isn't you would laugh at how pathetic this is. But you're not that person right now. You're the person for whom moving one leg is a real thing you did.

The other leg is still there. The floor is still distant. But something shifted.

You sit up. You count.

One. Two. Three. Your body wants to fall back. Four. Five. Six. This is stupid. Seven. Eight. Who counts to ten while sitting up. Nine. Ten.

You did it. You sat for ten seconds. The smallest possible victory. But your body is now vertical, which it wasn't before.

You type: "having a hard morning. can't get up."

You stare at it. Too honest? Too dramatic? They'll worry. They'll judge. They'll tell you to just get up, like that's something you haven't thought of.

You send it anyway. Then you wait, phone in hand, still horizontal.

Your feet touch the floor. It's cold. Real.

You're sitting on the edge of the bed now. Technically, you could still fall back. The bed is right behind you, gravitational, patient. But your feet are on the ground.

From here, standing is possible. Not easy. Not guaranteed. But possible.

What's the next smallest thing?

You're standing. Swaying slightly, but upright.

The room feels different from this angle. More real. More demanding. There are things to do here—clothes to put on, teeth to brush, a life to perform.

But you don't have to do all of them. You just have to do one.

Or not. You could sit back down. No one would know.

No. You're going to do this properly. Shower, get dressed, make the bed, have breakfast, be a normal person who does normal things.

You start the shower. The water is too cold, then too hot. You stand under it feeling nothing. The shampoo bottle is heavy. Everything takes twice as long.

By the time you're dried off, you're exhausted. More exhausted than before you started. The bed is right there. You haven't made it yet.

Maybe just sit for a second.

You're back in bed. It happened fast—one moment you were trying, the next you were horizontal again.

The failure settles over you like another blanket. You couldn't even do the basics. What's wrong with you?

The day continues outside. You're still here.

What is wrong with you? Normal people get out of bed. Normal people don't lie here feeling like the world is too heavy to face. You're lazy. You're broken. You're wasting your life.

The thoughts pile on. Each one true. Each one making it harder to move. The criticism doesn't motivate—it paralyzes. But it feels deserved, which is almost the same as feeling right.

You're still in bed. The attack continues.

Wait.

You've heard this before. This exact script. The "what's wrong with you" voice that shows up when you're already down and pushes you further.

It's not new information. It's just the same loop, playing again.

Noticing it doesn't make it stop. But it does create a tiny gap between you and the voice. A moment where you can see it as a pattern instead of the truth.

You try a different voice. Not cheerful—that would be fake. Just... less cruel.

"This is hard. It's hard for a reason. You're not lazy—you're struggling. And struggling while lying in bed still counts as struggling."

The words feel foreign. Unearned. But also true?

You're still in bed. But the weight is slightly different.

Your phone buzzes.

"that sucks. can I call you? or do you want me to just come over and sit with you?"

Someone knows. Someone responded without judgment. The weight doesn't lift, but it shifts slightly—less alone, less invisible.

You could say yes. You could say no. You could not respond and just lie here knowing someone out there knows.

What's the smallest thing that would count as doing something?

Not the shower. Not getting dressed. Not the full routine that normal people do without thinking. Just... one thing. The minimum viable morning.

Water. You could drink water. That's a thing.
Teeth. You could brush your teeth.
Pants. You could put on pants.

Pick one. The smallest one you can actually do.

You did one thing.

It wasn't much. In the grand scheme of a day, it was almost nothing. But you moved. You did something besides lie there.

Your body is still heavy. The day is still out there. But you're no longer at zero. You're at one.

One is enough to build on. Or one is enough for today. Both are valid.

Two things. Water and teeth. Or pants and water. Whatever combination you managed.

You're not dressed. You haven't showered. By most standards, you're not ready for anything. But you're more ready than you were an hour ago.

The momentum is fragile—you can feel it. One wrong move and you're back in bed. But right now, you're moving.

This is enough.

Not enough by some external standard. Not enough to feel proud or accomplished. But enough for what you could do today.

You're vertical. You did something. The day will continue with or without your full participation, and today you're offering partial participation.

That's real. That counts. It has to count.

If you can do one thing, you should be able to do everything.

That's how it works, right? Normal people don't stop after drinking water. Normal people get dressed and go to work and live their lives. If you can't do that, what's the point of the water?

**[The all-or-nothing pattern is taking over]**

The water feels pointless now. The momentum drains away. You're back to thinking about everything you're not doing instead of the one thing you did.

You fell back, but you're trying again. Gentler this time.

No big plans. No full routine. Just: what can you do from here?

The bed is warm. The world is hard. But somewhere between "do everything" and "do nothing" there's a middle path. You just have to find it.

You're not alone anymore.

They're here—on the phone or in person. Not fixing anything, just present. Witness to the struggle. It's embarrassing and it's also a relief.

"I know it's hard," they say. "What do you need?"

You don't know what you need. But the question opens something.

They don't do it for you. But they're there while you do it.

You sit up. They wait. You put your feet on the floor. They say nothing. You stand, and they nod, and somehow that small acknowledgment matters.

You're doing the same things you couldn't do alone. The physics haven't changed. But having a witness makes the impossible slightly more possible.

You're still in bed. Hours have passed or minutes—it's hard to tell.

The day is happening out there. You're not part of it. The weight hasn't lifted; if anything, it's settled deeper.

This is what depression looks like from the inside. Not dramatic. Not visible. Just... immobile.

The tears come. You're not sure why now—nothing changed. Just suddenly you're crying.

It's not dramatic crying. Just quiet, leaking tears and a tightness in your chest that finally releases. All the weight you've been lying under, finally expressed.

After a while, it stops. You're still in bed. But something is different. Lighter? Emptier? You're not sure.

You're up. Partially. You did some things, not all things. The day will be incomplete, reduced, smaller than it was supposed to be.

But you're not still in bed. That's the difference between today and the version of today where you never moved at all.

Partial is not failure. Partial is what you could do. And you did it.

You stayed in bed. The day happened without you.

There will be consequences—things undone, people wondering, the accumulated weight of another lost day. But right now, in this moment, you survived it.

Survival isn't progress. But it's also not nothing. You're still here. Tomorrow exists. That's something.

endings.title: Small Wins Add Up
endings.text:
You got up. You did things. Not all the things—maybe not even most of them. But you broke the inertia.

You didn't leap out of bed with energy. You ground through the heaviness one micro-step at a time.

You lowered the bar to something you could actually do. You built momentum instead of demanding everything at once. You let partial count.

Once you're moving, even slightly, it gets easier. You found the entry point.

Next: Tomorrow morning, commit to one tiny step. Sit up. That's it.

transferPrompts.default: Tomorrow: sit up. That's the whole task. Momentum follows.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you demand the full performance when the smallest step would work?
What was the smallest thing that actually moved you?

endings.title: Partial Is Real
endings.text:
You're up. Partially. You did some things, not all things. The day will be smaller than it was supposed to be.

But you're not still in bed. The difference between 'stayed in bed all day' and 'got up and did one thing' is real, even if it doesn't feel like much.

You accepted partial as valid. You didn't let all-or-nothing thinking collapse your progress. You found a workable middle ground.

'Not enough' is often a lie. You did something. That counts.

Next: Define 'enough' before you start tomorrow. Stick to it.

transferPrompts.default: Define 'enough' tonight. Write it down. Don't let the goalposts move.

reflectionPrompts: Where else does 'not enough' erase what you actually did?
What let you accept partial this time?

endings.title: Supported Movement
endings.text:
You told someone. They showed up. The weight shifted.

You didn't carry it alone. That changed things. The impossible became slightly less impossible with a witness.

Next: Text someone tonight: 'Check on me tomorrow morning.'

transferPrompts.default: Set up a morning check-in tonight. Before you need it.

reflectionPrompts: When else do you carry it alone and stay stuck?
What made reaching out possible this time?

endings.title: Kinder Voice
endings.text:
The attack voice was running. You tried a different one.

Yelling at yourself didn't work. It never does on these mornings. You found something else.

Next: When you hear 'what's wrong with you'—say 'I'm struggling. That's what this is.'

transferPrompts.default: When you hear 'what's wrong with you': say 'I'm struggling. That's what this is.'

reflectionPrompts: When does the attack voice actually help you move?
What worked instead?

endings.title: After the Fall
endings.text:
You collapsed back into bed. And then you got up again.

That second attempt is the move almost nobody makes. Most people who fall back stay down. You didn't. You found a gentler approach, a smaller step, a different way.

Your brain just logged: 'Falling doesn't mean staying down.' That's data it couldn't get from staying collapsed.

Next: If you collapse tomorrow, 5-minute timer. Then one smaller step.

transferPrompts.default: If you collapse tomorrow: 5-minute timer, then one smaller step.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you treat a setback as final when it doesn't have to be?
What made the second attempt possible?

endings.title: Still Processing
endings.text:
You're up. You're not sure if it counts. The day exists and you're participating in it, at least minimally.

Maybe this is progress. Maybe it's just going through motions. You genuinely don't know.

That uncertainty is okay. Not everything resolves into clear success or failure. Sometimes you just do the thing and wait to see what it meant.

You got up despite not knowing if it would help. You're sitting with ambiguity instead of forcing a verdict.

Next: Check in tonight—sometimes morning meaning gets clearer by evening.

transferPrompts.default: Check in tonight—sometimes morning meaning gets clearer by evening.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you force a verdict before the data is in?
What happens if you let this settle without labeling it?

endings.title: Undercutting the Win
endings.text:
You got up. You did things. And then the critic voice turned it all into evidence of failure.

'That wasn't enough.' 'Normal people don't struggle with this.' 'You should be doing more.'

The progress was real. The attack is a distortion. But the distortion feels more true right now.

You did something and then let the critic erase it. That's the trap. The goalposts moved after you scored.

Next: Notice when 'not enough' appears. Ask: 'Is this observation or attack?'

transferPrompts.default: Write down what you actually did. Just facts. No commentary. Read it tonight.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you let the critic erase real progress?
What did the attack voice say?

smallestBetterMove.description: Use self-compassion to counter the self-attack

endings.title: Still Here
endings.text:
You stayed in bed. The day happened without you.

There will be consequences—things undone, people wondering. But right now, you survived it.

On the worst days, survival is what's available. You're still here. Tomorrow exists.

Today was one day. It doesn't define the pattern.

Next: Tonight, set up one thing. Alarm across the room. Text from a friend. Something.

transferPrompts.default: Tonight: set up one thing. Alarm. Text. Reward. Something.

reflectionPrompts: What's the smallest step that might actually work tomorrow?
What was the barrier today?

smallestBetterMove.description: Put just one leg off the bed—the smallest possible step

endings.title: Tomorrow Exists
endings.text:
Today didn't work. The weight was too heavy, the steps too impossible, the gap between bed and world too wide.

But tomorrow is another day. The heaviness might be different. The barrier might be lower. What was impossible today might be merely hard tomorrow.

Days vary. One bad morning doesn't lock in every morning.

You're framing this as temporary, not permanent. That counts.

Next: Set up one tiny thing tonight. Alarm. Text. Reward.

transferPrompts.default: Tonight: set up one tiny thing. Alarm. Text. Reward.

reflectionPrompts: What's one thing you could set up tonight?
What would help tomorrow be different?

endings.title: Emptied Out
endings.text:
You cried. Something that was stuck got unstuck.

You're still in bed. The day is still happening without you. But the weight feels different now—not lighter exactly, but looser. Less solid.

You allowed the release instead of suppressing it. The body needed to discharge before the mind could engage.

Next: If tears are close, let them come. Then try one small step after.

transferPrompts.default: If tears are close, let them come. Then one small step.

reflectionPrompts: What shifted after the release?

endings.title: Too Much Too Fast
endings.text:
You tried to do everything. The full routine. The normal morning. And it crashed you harder than doing nothing.

You demanded the full version when your capacity was diminished. The overreach burned through what little energy you had. You ended up worse than if you'd done less.

Forcing through works for some things. This isn't one of them.

Next: Before starting anything, ask: 'Can I do even less?'

transferPrompts.default: Before starting: 'Can I do even less? What's the minimum viable version?'

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you demand everything and get nothing?
What would the smallest version have been?

smallestBetterMove.description: Do just one tiny task—drink water—instead of the full routine

endings.title: Seeing the Loop
endings.text:
You caught it. The thought pattern that was playing—the self-attack script, the all-or-nothing demand—you saw it as a pattern instead of the truth.

That's not the same as stopping it. The pattern still ran. But there was a gap, a moment of awareness, where you and the thought were separate things.

You noticed you were in a familiar loop. You created distance. You acted (or rested) with awareness instead of fusion.

Awareness doesn't require fixing. Sometimes just seeing the pattern is the work.

Next: See if you can catch the loop even earlier—at the first 'what's wrong with you.'

llmHints.scenarioContext: Person with depression trying to get out of bed in the morning. Core challenges: activation energy, self-attack patterns, all-or-nothing thinking, inertia, self-negotiation, and finding workable next steps when everything feels too hard. The scenario is about micro-momentum, not dramatic breakthroughs.
coachingFocus: Activation barriers: how depression makes simple tasks feel impossible
Self-attack vs self-compassion: different inner voices lead to different outcomes
All-or-nothing thinking: the trap of 'if I can't do everything, why do anything'
Threshold lowering: finding the smallest possible step that still counts
Recovery after setback: falling back into bed doesn't have to be permanent
Partial progress as real progress: redefining success for low-energy days
Connection and support: using others as activation scaffolding
Metacognition: noticing thought patterns while they're happening
debriefPrompts: What was the hardest moment—where did you feel most stuck?
Did you notice the self-attack voice? What did it say?
What was the smallest step you found that actually worked?
If you collapsed back, what helped you try again (or what would have helped)?
What does 'enough' look like on a day like this?
Did reaching out or accepting support feel different than going it alone?

activation.whenStrong: You broke through the inertia. That's the hardest part. Use this skill in other stuck moments.
activation.whenWeak: The activation barrier was too high. Tomorrow, try setting up scaffolding the night before.
activation.practiceHint: Before bed, put one thing in place to make tomorrow's first step easier.

threshold_lowering.whenStrong: You found the smallest workable step. This skill works everywhere depression creates barriers.
threshold_lowering.whenWeak: You set the bar too high. Ask: What's even smaller? Can I do 10% of that?
threshold_lowering.practiceHint: Whatever step you're planning, ask: What's the minimum viable version?

self_compassion.whenStrong: You used a kinder voice. That's strategic, not soft. Criticism paralyzes; kindness mobilizes.
self_compassion.whenWeak: The self-attack voice won. It feels true but it's a trap.
self_compassion.practiceHint: When the critic starts, name it: 'That's the attack voice.' Then try something else.

recovery.whenStrong: You came back after falling. That's one of the rarest and most valuable skills.
recovery.whenWeak: When you fell back, you stayed down. Recovery is learnable.
recovery.practiceHint: If you collapse, set a 5-minute timer. When it goes off, try one smaller step.

persistence.whenStrong: You kept going through the heaviness. That builds capacity for next time.
persistence.whenWeak: You stopped before you wanted to. Tomorrow, try committing to one more step than feels possible.
persistence.practiceHint: When you want to stop, commit to 2 more minutes. Just 2.

support_seeking.whenStrong: You used connection. Depression says isolate; support is acting against the illness.
support_seeking.whenWeak: You went it alone when support was available. Asking isn't weakness—it's data.
support_seeking.practiceHint: Set up a morning check-in text with someone before you go to sleep.

micro_progress.detected: You built momentum through tiny steps. This is how activation works in depression.
micro_progress.nextStep: Apply this in another area: find the smallest possible step and start there.

threshold_lowered.detected: You found the minimum viable version. This skill transfers to any stuck moment.
threshold_lowered.nextStep: Before your next hard task, ask: What's 10% of this?

recovery_success.detected: You came back after collapse. Most people stay down. You didn't.
recovery_success.nextStep: Trust this skill. If you fall tomorrow, remember: the second try is always available.

compassion_applied.detected: You used a kinder voice instead of the critic. That's real work.
compassion_applied.nextStep: Notice when you're yelling at yourself. Try something else instead.

support_utilized.detected: You used connection to enable action. That's strength, not weakness.
support_utilized.nextStep: Set up support systems before you need them. Morning check-ins. Accountability.

self_attack_spiral.detected: The self-attack voice took over. It feels true but it's a trap.
self_attack_spiral.nextStep: Name the voice: 'That's the critic, not the truth.' See if naming creates distance.

perfectionism_trap.detected: All-or-nothing thinking collapsed partial progress into nothing.
perfectionism_trap.nextStep: Define 'enough' before you start tomorrow. Write it down. Stick to it.

overreach_collapse.detected: You tried to do everything and crashed. The full routine was too much.
overreach_collapse.nextStep: Tomorrow, start smaller. Ask: Is this the minimum viable version?

avoidance_at_threshold.detected: You couldn't cross the activation barrier. The gap was too wide.
avoidance_at_threshold.nextStep: Set up scaffolding tonight: one small thing in place to make tomorrow easier.

stuckMoment.description: Waking up and being unable to get out of bed due to overwhelming heaviness and inertia
stuckMoment.trigger: Morning alarm or waking naturally, facing the transition from bed to the day
stuckMoment.internalExperience: Body feels like lead, brain foggy, everything seems too hard, self-criticism loops, desire to disappear back into sleep

realWorldAnalogs: Getting out of bed on a low-energy morning
Starting work when you don't want to
Leaving the house when everything feels too hard
Beginning exercise when your body wants to stay still
Taking a shower when depression makes hygiene feel impossible

patternLabelMap.experiential_avoidance: You pulled back from the hard part
patternLabelMap.micro_step_success: You found a move small enough to work
patternLabelMap.overforcing: You pushed and your system pushed back
patternLabelMap.recovery_success: You came back after pulling away
patternLabelMap.flexible_response: You adjusted when it didn't work
patternLabelMap.distress_tolerated: You stayed through the hard part
patternLabelMap.direct_communication: You asked for what you needed

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You built momentum through sequence: sit, feet down, stand, one task.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'I can get up when the bar is low enough.' That's data it couldn't get from staying down.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Tomorrow: sit up, feet down, stand, one task. Same sequence.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: Once you're moving, even slightly, momentum exists. You found the entry point.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The sequence gets easier. The barrier gets lower.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: When the day feels impossible, find the smallest move that still counts.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You found the smallest possible step and started there—one leg, ten seconds, just water.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: You proved that 'pathetically small' can still move you. The bar doesn't have to be impressive to work.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Find the step your brain can't say no to. That's the real entry point.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: The bar was survivable. You met it.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: You keep finding entry points when the day looks impossible.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: When stuck: what's the minimum viable version? Do that.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The attack voice was running. You tried a different one.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Yelling didn't work. It never does on these mornings. You tried something else.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: When you hear 'what's wrong with you': say 'I'm struggling. That's what this is.'
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: The attack freezes you. You found something that didn't.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The other voice gets easier to find.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Notice when you're yelling at yourself. Try something else.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You told someone. They showed up. The weight shifted.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: You didn't carry it alone. That's not weakness—that's data. The weight moved when someone else knew.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Text someone tonight: 'Check on me tomorrow morning.'
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: Alone, you stayed stuck. With a witness, you moved.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Asking gets less weird. The isolation loses its grip.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: When you can't move alone, tell someone.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You collapsed back into bed. And then you got up again.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Most people who collapse stay down. You just proved that's not required. Your brain logged: 'I can recover.'
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: If you collapse tomorrow, give yourself 5 minutes. Then try a smaller step.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: The second attempt is the hidden skill. You did it.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Collapse becomes a pause, not a verdict.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: When you fall back, the second try is always available.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You stayed in bed. The weight was too heavy today.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Your brain logged: 'Confirmed: too hard.' That makes tomorrow start harder. But tomorrow is another day.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Tonight: set up one tiny thing. Alarm across the room. Text from a friend. Something.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: Today was one day. It doesn't define the pattern.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The barrier keeps getting higher. But you can interrupt that.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You demanded the full routine. It crashed you harder than doing nothing.
routeInterpretations.dominantUserFacingPatternLabel: You set the bar too high and couldn't clear it
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Forcing through works for some things. This isn't one of them. You burned through what energy you had and ended up worse.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Before starting anything, ask: Can I do even less?
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: The overreach was the problem, not you.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: You keep burning out at the start and never building momentum.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: When capacity is low, go smaller, not harder.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You let the self-attack pattern run. It paralyzed you.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: The attack voice sounds like it's trying to help. It's not. It froze you in place.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: When the attack starts, name it: 'That's the critic, not the truth.'
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: The critic made movement impossible. That's what it does.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The critic becomes the default voice. Every hard morning starts with an attack.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Notice when the critic is running. Don't let it finish the script.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: All-or-nothing thinking collapsed partial progress into nothing.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: You did something. Then the 'not enough' voice made it count as nothing. That's the trap.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: When 'not enough' appears, ask: Is this observation or all-or-nothing?
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: Partial got erased. That's the all-or-nothing pattern at work.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Nothing ever counts. Every attempt gets canceled.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Define 'enough' before you start. Don't let the goalposts move.

insightBeats.insightText: You're yelling at yourself for not being able to do the thing. The yelling is making the thing harder.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: The attack sounds like motivation. It's not. It's a freeze response dressed up as discipline.
insightBeats.tryNextCue: Name it: 'That's the attack voice.' Don't argue with it. Just label it.

microInterventions.why: Labeling creates distance. Distance creates choice.

microInterventions.text: Notice where you feel it in your body.
microInterventions.why: The attack lives in your body. Noticing it loosens the grip.

insightBeats.insightText: Under the covers, the day can't find you. But it's still out there. And each minute makes re-entry harder.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: The relief is real. So is the cost. Every minute under there teaches your brain that the day is too much.
insightBeats.tryNextCue: Uncover your face. Just your face. Let the light in.

microInterventions.text: Pull the covers below your chin. That's it.
microInterventions.why: Tiny reversal. You're not hiding anymore.
Delay the permanent decision. See if it shifts.

insightBeats.insightText: Your brain just said: if you can't do everything, why do anything? That's the trap. Partial counts. One thing counts.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: All-or-nothing erases partial wins. You did something. The voice is lying about what counts.
insightBeats.tryNextCue: Say: 'One thing is real.' Don't let the bar move.

microInterventions.text: Name one thing you already did. Out loud.
microInterventions.why: You're fighting the erasure. The thing happened.

microInterventions.text: Ask: 'Who set this bar? Was it me or the pattern?'
microInterventions.why: The bar is a lie. You can set a different one.

insightBeats.insightText: You fell back. And now you're trying again. That second attempt is the move most people don't make.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: Collapse usually wins. You just proved it doesn't have to. Your brain is logging new data right now.

microInterventions.text: Go even smaller than before. What's the minimum?
microInterventions.why: The first bar was too high. Find a lower one.

microInterventions.text: Say: 'I came back.' That's the win.
microInterventions.why: The return is the skill. Everything else is bonus.
